name: Tries and Prefix Trees
intent: Understand how a trie answers "everything that starts with these letters" in a number of steps that follows the prefix and the answer, not the size of the key set, what that costs in memory, and how compressed tries and sorted arrays change the trade.
scenario: A search box suggests completions over 10,000 keys. The user has typed "taka". A hash map cannot help with a prefix, so scanning every key costs 11,945 character steps. Binary search over the keys kept in sorted order costs 238. A trie walks 4 nodes and reads what is below: 102 steps for all 48 matches, and 21 if the box only wants the first 10. But on 10,000 random 8-letter ids the trie has 58,243 nodes for 80,000 characters, and 1,514,318 child slots if every node holds an array for a to z.
problem: A hash map is built for one question, "is exactly this key here", and a prefix is not a key: the hash of "tak" says nothing about where "taka" or "takoma" went. So prefix questions (autocomplete, routing tables, spell-check, "all paths under /api/v2/") degrade to scanning everything. A trie stores the keys letter by letter in a tree so that all keys sharing a prefix share a path. That makes prefix lookup cheap, but it is not free: a naive trie spends a node per letter, and nodes are much bigger than letters. Developers either reach for a trie where a sorted array is cheaper and simpler, or never reach for it and scan.

howItWorks.title: One edge per letter, one path per prefix
howItWorks.text: A trie (from retrieval, also called a prefix tree) is a tree where each edge is labelled with a character and the path from the root spells a prefix. The keys "tea", "ten" and "to" share the node for "t", and "tea" and "ten" also share "te". A flag on a node says that a key ends there, so "tea" can be stored while "te" is only a prefix. Inserting a key of length L walks or creates at most L nodes.

howItWorks.title: Lookup follows the key, not the key set
howItWorks.text: To check a key, follow its letters from the root: L steps, whether the trie holds a hundred keys or a hundred million. A hash map also needs time proportional to L to hash the key, so for exact match the two are the same order, and the hash map is usually the faster one in practice. The trie's real gift is the next step: after walking the prefix you stand on the node that roots every key with that prefix.

howItWorks.title: Prefix search is the walk plus the subtree
howItWorks.text: Walk the L letters of the prefix, then read the subtree below that node, visiting children in letter order to get sorted suggestions. The cost is L plus the nodes you visit, and you can stop after the first 10 results without touching the rest. That is why autocomplete over 10,000 keys costs 21 steps for the first 10 while a scan costs 3,262. If the answer is huge (a one-letter prefix with 1,245 matches) the subtree read dominates, and a sorted array that reads matching keys one after another can be cheaper than the trie's inner nodes.

howItWorks.title: The memory bill
howItWorks.text: A trie spends one node per distinct prefix. Keys that share beginnings (words, URL paths, IP prefixes) share nodes. Keys that do not (random ids, hashes) get a node per letter, so 10,000 ids of 8 letters make 58,243 nodes. If each node holds an array of 26 child slots, that is 1,514,318 slots for 80,000 stored letters: nearly 19 slots per letter, almost all empty. Storing children in a small map or sorted list instead cuts the slots to the number of real edges, at the cost of a slower step.

howItWorks.title: Compress, or use a sorted array
howItWorks.text: A compressed trie (radix tree, Patricia trie) merges chains of single-child nodes into one edge labelled with a whole string, keeping only the root, word ends and branch points: 12,704 nodes instead of 58,243 for the ids. IP routers use tries of this family for longest-prefix match, and some search engines store term dictionaries as finite state machines that also share suffixes. And for static data a sorted array with binary search is often the better answer: no pointers, one contiguous block, 238 steps instead of 11,945 for the same prefix, and it supports range scans. A trie earns its place when the key set changes constantly, when you need the first few results fast, or when you need to branch on the next letter (longest prefix, typo-tolerant walks).

pros: Prefix lookup in a number of steps that follows the prefix length and the answer size, not the number of keys
Results come out in key order, and the walk can stop after the first few suggestions
Shared prefixes are stored once, which helps for words, paths and IP prefixes
Supports longest-prefix match and walking letter by letter, which a hash map cannot do
cons: A naive trie costs a node per distinct prefix, and a node is far bigger than the letter it holds
Pointer chasing makes a trie slower in practice than a sorted array or hash map at the same step count
Random or high-entropy keys (ids, hashes) share almost no prefixes, so there is little to save
When the answer is huge, reading the inner nodes can cost more than reading sorted keys
whenToUse: Autocomplete, spell suggestion and command completion where the key set changes and only the first few results matter
Longest-prefix matching: IP routing tables, URL or path routers, phone number prefixes
Keys with long shared beginnings, where storing each prefix once saves real memory
whenNotToUse: Exact-match lookups only: a hash map is simpler and usually faster
Static data with prefix queries: a sorted array and binary search needs no pointers and often wins
Random ids or hashes: almost nothing is shared, so the trie is a large tree of single-child chains
Very large key sets in memory-tight services, unless a compressed or on-disk structure is used
pitfalls: Using a trie because "prefix search" was said, without measuring a sorted array: for data that rarely changes, binary search plus a short forward scan is about as fast and far smaller
Array-per-node children for a big alphabet: 26 slots is bad, and for Unicode it is hopeless. Use a map, a sorted list of edges, or a compressed trie
Counting steps but not nodes: the node count (and its bytes per node) is the real cost, and it grows with the number of distinct prefixes, not with the number of keys
Expecting the first few suggestions to be the best ones: letter order is not relevance. Real autocomplete usually stores a score or the top suggestions per node, or re-ranks the candidates afterwards
Forgetting the short-prefix case: after one letter the subtree may hold a large share of all keys. Cap the result count, or precompute the top suggestions for short prefixes
Case, accents and Unicode: "Ünal" and "unal" are different paths unless you normalize keys first, and one visible character can be several code points
Treating insert and delete as free: deleting a key must prune nodes that no other key uses, or the trie only ever grows

roles.label: User typing
roles.description: Types a prefix one letter at a time and expects suggestions after every key press.

roles.label: Hash map or list
roles.description: Finds exact keys quickly but has no notion of a prefix: it must examine every key.

roles.label: Sorted keys
roles.description: Keys in letter order: binary search finds the first match, then matches follow one after another.

roles.label: Trie
roles.description: A node per distinct prefix: walk the letters, then read the subtree.

roles.label: Compressed trie
roles.description: The same tree with single-child chains merged into one edge.

quiz.question: An autocomplete box needs the first 10 keys that start with what the user typed, over 10,000 keys held in a hash map. Why is that expensive, and what does a trie change?
options: It has no prefix structure, so it checks every key; a trie walks the typed letters and reads a few nodes.
A hash map cannot store text keys at all, so a trie is the only structure that can hold strings of letters.
A hash map returns results in random order, and a trie is faster only because it sorts the keys at lookup time.
A hash map uses too much memory per key, and a trie always uses less memory than a hash map does.
quiz.explanation: A hash maps an exact key to a bucket, and a prefix has no bucket, so every key must be examined. A trie keeps all keys with a shared start under one node, so the work follows the prefix length and the number of results wanted. The trie does not always use less memory.

quiz.question: 10,000 random 8-letter ids are inserted into a trie whose nodes each hold an array of 26 child slots. The trie has 58,243 nodes. What is the main lesson?
options: The trie is the right structure, because 58,243 nodes is fewer than the 80,000 letters stored.
Random keys share few prefixes, so nodes near one per letter and most slots stay empty.
The alphabet should be larger so that more of the keys end up sharing prefixes with each other.
Memory use of a trie does not depend on the keys at all, only on the size of the alphabet.
quiz.explanation: Sharing is what makes a trie compact. Random ids differ from the first letter or two on, so most nodes sit on single-child chains: 58,243 nodes for 80,000 letters, over a million mostly empty slots. A compressed trie, a map for children, a sorted array, or a hash map suits such keys better.

quiz.question: A sorted array of keys and a trie both answer prefix queries. When is the sorted array likely to be the better choice?
options: When keys are inserted and deleted thousands of times per second, all day long.
When you must follow the next letter of a key to find a longest-prefix match.
When keys rarely change and you want one compact block: binary search, then read on.
When prefix queries must stop after the very first result without reading any further at all.
quiz.explanation: Keys in one contiguous block need no pointers, binary search finds the first match in about log n comparisons, and matches sit next to each other. A trie pays off when the set changes constantly, when you walk letter by letter, or when the first few results matter and the subtree is small.
